newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa seeks better trade deal from EU.
newsitem.headline: South Africa seeks better trade deal from EU.

text.p: South Africa said on Tuesday it was seeking a better deal in trade talks with the European Union to address regional concerns and the need for "asymmetrical" trade liberalisation.

But South Africa's ambassador to the EU, Eltie Links, head of his country's negotiating team, said Pretoria had not rejected outright an earlier EU negotiating mandate, adding that there was willingness on both sides to reach agreement.
"Our differences will inevitably raise eyebrows and raise tones of voices. What must be understood, however, is that there is an underlying seriousness on both sides," he said.
Links told reporters the talks scheduled for Friday and Saturday in Pretoria should set the stage for more intensive and detailed negotiations.

Faizel Ismail, director of foreign trade relations in the department of trade and industry, said South Africa's negotiating mandate, formally to be presented at the talks, would address several concerns:
- Any trade deal should be asymmetrical, with the EU opening up a far greater percentage of its markets to South Africa than South Africa would be required to open to the EU.
- An agreement had to take into account South Africa's neighbours in the Southern African Customs Union (SACU) who could otherwise lose valuable customs levies.
- The EU had to pay more attention to the impact of any agreement on the wider Southern African Development Community (SADC), which plans its own internal free trade agreement in eight years.
- A package of measures was needed to help South Africa adjust to further trade liberalisation.
- The EU should rethink its current proposal on agricultural products which would exclude almost 40 percent of South African farm exports.
The negotiations were put back on track last month when South Africa broke an impasse by outlining its mandate, or negotiating position.
The EU set out its mandate in March 1996 and has accused Pretoria of dragging its feet since then.
Brussels has refused post-apartheid South Africa full accession to the Lome Convention which grants favourable access to its markets to developing countries in Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific.
